bio.en: Jerry Colonna is one of the world's most respected executive coaches, co-founder and CEO of Reboot, and a former venture capitalist (Flatiron Partners) and author of Reboot and Reunion; he helps leaders do the inner work of becoming better humans.
bio.zh: Jerry Colonna 是全球最受尊敬的髙管教练之一，也是 Reboot 的联合创始人兼 CEO、前风险投资家（Flatiron Partners）以及《Reboot》《Reunion》的作者；他帮助领导者通过内在修炼成为更好的人。

summary.en: Jerry challenges the entrepreneurial culture of bullshitting ourselves that 'everything's up and to the right,' and offers his piercing question—'how have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want?'—as a way to reclaim agency. He discusses the dangers of an unexamined 'growth mindset,' why self-inquiry and busyness are worth confronting, and a simple equation his team uses to cultivate great leaders. The conversation is unusually raw and human, and aimed at making you a better person, partner, and leader.
summary.zh: Jerry 质疑创业圈里“一切都在向右上增长”的自我欺骗，并抛出一个犀利的问题——“我如何共谋创造了那些我说自己不想要的局面？”——以此重新拿回主动权。他谈到了不加检视的“成长型思维”的危险、为何值得直面自我审视与忙碌，以及他的团队用来培养卓越领导者的一个简单公式。这期对话出奇地真实、有人情味，目标是让你成为更好的人、更好的伴侣与更好的领导者。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: We're socialized to bullshit not only ourselves, but everybody else, especially in the entrepreneurial community. All our companies are moving up into the right. Every product is working. We don't really have any problems because we're crushing it, and that's just a lie. The question that I often ask is how have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want. The purpose of this question is actually to evoke your own agency. A perfect example of that would be, I say I don't want to feel busy all the time, but the truth of the matter is I feel really unnerved and disconcerted if my agenda isn't jam-packed. So if you want to create a high-functioning team, do your work, and it starts with the person who has the most power.
turns.zh: 我们被社会化训练得不仅对自己撒谎，还会对他人撒谎——尤其是在创业圈。我们总说自己的公司蒸蒸日上、产品无懈可击，仿佛自己无比成功。但这不过是自欺欺人。而我常问的问题是，自己为何会助长了那些自己明明不愿看到的现状？这种追问的核心其实是激发你的自主行动力。举个典型例子：我嘴上说不愿时刻处于忙碌状态，但真相是——如果日程表没有排得满满当当，我反而会感到焦虑不安。所以若想打造一支高效运作的团队，首先得从拥有最大话语权的人做起。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, thanks for having me, Lenny. It's really a delight to meet you and to be with you today.
turns.zh: 嗯，感谢邀请，伦尼。很高兴今天能与你见面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to start with a very classic Jerry Colonna piece of advice that I've heard you share in other places, and I just want more people to hear this advice, and this is a question that you ask people when things aren't going their way, and I'll give you a hint. The question contains the word complicit.
turns.zh: 我想先分享杰瑞·科洛纳（Jerry Colonna）的一条经典建议，我曾在其他场合听你提过，我希望更多人能听到这个建议。这是当事情进展不顺时，你会问人们的一个问题，我给你个提示，这个问题里有个词叫"同谋"。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you share this question and why it's so important to ask this of yourself?
turns.zh: 你能分享一下这个问题，以及为什么问自己这个问题如此重要吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: The question that I often ask is how have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want? And if it's helpful, let me break down the question a little bit.
turns.zh: 我常问的问题是，我是如何在不知不觉中促成了自己口中所说的"不想要"的处境？如果方便的话，我可以稍微解析一下这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: So I purposely chose the word complicit because complicit does not mean responsible, and that's a really important distinction. And as I often say, to understand the word complicit, think of the word accomplice. As I will share, you are driving the getaway car, you're not sticking up the bank teller. The second half of that question is I say I don't want. And sometimes people hear that question and they interpret it as, how have I been responsible for the shit in my life? And that is not the purpose of this question. The purpose of this question is actually to evoke your own agency, is to look at the ways in which you may have been diluting yourself. (00:05:56): A perfect example of that would be, I say I don't want to feel busy all the time, but the truth of the matter is I feel really unnerved and disconcerted if my agenda isn't jam-packed. And the reason that this is all really important is part of my approach not only to coaching, but to the process of growing up, is to use what I call radical self-inquiry, to really cut through our own delusions and say, how does it serve me to feel completely busy to the point where I feel exhausted? And perhaps there's another more conscious way of getting that feeling than feeling like crap all the time.
turns.zh: 所以我特意选用"同谋"这个词，因为"同谋"并不意味着责任，这是一个非常重要的区分。正如我常说的，理解"同谋"这个词，可以想想"同谋"这个词。举个例子，你在驾驶逃逸车辆，而不是抢劫银行柜员。问题的后半部分是"我说我不想要"。有时人们听到这个问题，会把它理解成"我对生活中的糟糕事负责吗？"但这不是这个问题的目的。这个问题的目的是唤醒你的自主意识，审视你可能在削弱自己的地方。（00:05:56）：一个典型的例子是，我说我不想总是感到忙碌，但事实是，如果我的日程不排得满满的，我就会感到不安和困惑。这一切之所以重要，是因为我不仅在教练工作中，而且在成长过程中，都采用一种我称之为"激进自我探索"的方法，真正打破我们的幻觉，问自己：把自己累得精疲力竭，到底有什么好处？也许还有更明智的方式来获得那种感觉，而不是一直感觉糟糕透顶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to something that I hear you. You have this equation that you and your firm use to think about how to create and cultivate great leaders, and it includes one of the variables is radical self-inquiry. Can you share this equation and just how you work with folks to build this in them?
turns.zh: 接下来我想谈谈我听到你提到的。你和你的公司有一个用来培养伟大领导者的公式，其中一个变量就是"激进自我探索"。能否分享一下这个公式，以及你们如何帮助人们培养这种能力？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Sure. I'll tell a little story about that. I remember one time I was, this is how the equation came to be. I was doing a talk, I think here in Boulder at Naropa University where I used to be on the board of trustees. It's a Buddhist university, and as is often the case, I'm winging it as I go and I'm walking around probably without shoes on because that's what I do. And there was a dry erase board behind me and I was trying to explain what it was that I do, what it was that I encourage people to do. And I jumped up at the board and I wrote practical skills. And in writing that, what I was trying to convey, what it is that people typically come to a coach for. They want to understand how to do their job. They want to understand how to live. They want to understand the how. (00:08:11): And then, I wrote plus, and then I sketched out radical self-inquiry. And I said in that moment, I said, "People will come and ask me how, and I will drive them crazy because I will say something like, tell me about your father, or tell me why you chose to be in the job you're in the first place, or tell me about your relationship to money, or tell me about your relationship to self-worth." And then, I expanded it and I put another plus sign and I said, "Shared experiences." And then, I drew an equals equation line underneath the whole thing, and I said, "Enhanced leadership plus greater resiliency." (00:09:05): And so, the equation is practical skills plus radical self-inquiry plus shared experiences, that is the process of actually talking about the craziness that goes on in your head equals greater leadership. That all makes sense. But then, there was this other piece, enhanced resilience. And when I do this on a dry erase board, I will often circle that phrase, and I say that is the purpose of this whole thing, because the truth is, if you follow my story at all, you know that in my late 30s, the depression that had really marked most of my life had gotten so bad that despite my outward success, I was suicidal and lost. (00:09:58): And I will turn to the audience and I say, "I get you want to be a great CEO, I get you want to be a great executive, but what I really care about is you not killing yourself in the process." So if we take a step back, the whole point of what we refer to as the equation really boils down to that point, how do we grow up and become the leaders, the adults we were born to be without feeling like crap?
turns.zh: 好的。让我讲个小故事吧。我记得有一次是这样的。当时我在博尔德的纳罗帕大学做演讲，我曾是该校董事会成员。这是一所佛教大学。像往常一样，我即兴发挥，可能当时还光着脚——反正我习惯这样。演讲台后面有一块白板，我试图解释自己所做的事情，以及我鼓励人们去做的事。我跳上白板写下“实用技能”。写下这几个字时，我想传达的是人们通常向教练寻求帮助的原因——他们想知道如何做好工作，如何生活，如何理解其中的奥秘。（00:08:11）然后我写了个加号，接着勾勒出“深度自我探索”。那一刻我说道："人们会来问我该怎么做，但我会把他们逼疯，因为我会问他们，比如：谈谈你的父亲吧，或者说说你当初为何选择这份工作，又或者谈谈你与金钱的关系，或者谈谈你对自尊的看法。"接着我又扩展了这个框架，加了一个加号，写道"共同经历"。然后我在整个框架下画了一条等号，写道"提升领导力+增强韧性"。（00:09:05）所以，这个等式就是：实用技能+深度自我探索+共同经历=提升领导力。这一切都说得通。但还有另一个关键点——增强韧性。当我在白板上写下这些时，我常常圈出这个短语，并强调这是整个过程的核心，因为说实话，如果你仔细听我的故事，就会知道我在30多岁时，困扰我多年的抑郁症愈发严重。尽管表面上事业成功，但我却陷入自杀倾向、迷失自我。（00:09:58）我会转向听众说："我知道你们想成为出色的CEO，优秀的高管，但我真正关心的是你们在追梦过程中别把自己逼疯了。"所以退一步来说，我们所说的这个等式，归根结底就是要学会成长，学会成为我们生来就该成为的领导者和成熟的成年人，而不必承受内心的煎熬。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's this huge implication here that a lot of people think that when they reach a certain point, become successful, make a certain amount of money, get a beautiful house, still be happy. And essentially what you're saying here is that's very often not the case. Maybe in most cases, not the case.
turns.zh: 这里有一个深刻的启示：许多人以为只要达到某个阶段、获得成功、赚到一定金额的钱、买到漂亮的房子，人生就会变得幸福。但你在这里要说的是，这往往并非事实。或许在大多数情况下根本不是这样。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: It's not only not the case, it's the big lie that we're socialized with since childhood. I remember one time I was on the road doing a talk for, I was promoting my first book, Reboot, and I was at, I think it's called the Fitler Club in Philadelphia. I was doing a fireside chat. And after talking with my conversation partner, a guy named Chris Fralic who was one of the co-founders at First Round, really, really good guy. We turned to the audience and there was a Q&A as there often is, and this young guy shoots his hand up and he introduces himself and he says, "I'm 19." And he looks over to his right and his mother's sitting there and he says, "And my mother brought me here," which I laughed. (00:11:40): And he said, "So what you're telling me is you don't have to be an asshole to be successful." And I could not think of a better summation of everything that I'm about than for a 19-year-old kid to look up and say, "You don't have to be an asshole to be successful." And of course, the corollary to that is you don't have to feel miserable just because you're trying to create a career.
turns.zh: 事实并非如此，这恰恰是我们从小就被灌输的谎言。我记得有一次我在路演宣传我的第一本书《重启》，当时是在费城的Fitler Club参加一场炉边谈话。与对话嘉宾——First Round的联合创始人Chris Fralic交谈结束后，我们转向观众，按惯例进行问答环节。这时一个年轻人举手自我介绍：“我19岁。”接着他扭头看向身旁的母亲说：“是我妈妈带我来的。”我不禁笑了起来。（00:11:40）他接着问：“所以你的意思是，不必为了成功而做个混蛋。”对于我所秉持的价值观来说，没有比这更贴切的总结了——一个19岁的年轻人能抬头说出“不必为了成功而做个混蛋”。当然，相反的道理也同样成立：你不必因为追逐事业而感到痛苦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As people start to think about this and think, okay, I feel like I've been heading in this direction of I just need to keep climbing the ladder, making more money, as they hear you talk, what's the pivot that folks should make in their mind around where they should actually be heading? What is a direction where they'll end up not wanting to kill themselves, in spite of being successful?
turns.zh: 人们开始思考这个问题时会想，嗯，我觉得自己一直朝着一个方向前进——就是不断攀登职场阶梯，赚更多钱。听你讲完后，我想问的是，人们应该在心里做出怎样的转变，才能真正找到自己该走的路？即便成功了，怎样才能不至于陷入自杀的绝望境地？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: To be clear, not everyone ends up in that level of depression, but the hack, if you will, is consciousness. So what do I mean by that? Part of what makes radical self-inquiry radical is we're socialized not to ask certain kinds of questions. So for example, someone says, "It's really important for me to be ambitious and achieve a particular goal." What's radical, a radical question to ask is, and what will that do for you? What is it that you believe being "successful" will do for you? How do you define success? Where does that come from? (00:13:30): In Reboot, my first book, I tell the story of what I refer to as my pursuit of lemon drops. And briefly, when I was a boy, there was a lot... I grew up with an enormous amount of chaos and insecurity, financial and otherwise. And a big source of stability in my life were my mother's parents, my grandfather and grandmother. And Grandpa Guido, who was an ice man and emigrated from southern Italy in early 20th century, always seemed to have, well, he had this endless supply of lemon drops, and they were always kept in this green pantry outside of the kitchen. And for me, the stability and what I considered wealth seemed to match to this notion of this endless supply of lemon drops. And when I got to my 30s and I was outwardly successful and I was a hot shot BC, I had lemon drops, but I didn't feel safe, which was a mindful. (00:15:02): And so, I told that story in Reboot as part of my exploration into the core question of how did my relationship to money shape my career choices, shape my school choices, shape my own sense of safety and self-worth? So long-winded response to your question, what I encourage people to do is to ask themselves these kinds of questions so that they can raise their level of consciousness so that they can be in the driver's seat of their lives and not some learned behavior that they developed as a child to answer perhaps their parents or grandparents' anxieties.
turns.zh:
说白了，并非所有人都会陷入那种程度的抑郁，但关键在于——如果你愿意称之为"觉醒"的话。那么我这么说是什么意思呢？激进的自我探索之所以激进，部分原因在于我们被社会化成不愿提出某些类型的问题。比如，有人会说："对自己有雄心、达成特定目标真的很重要。"而激进的问题应该是——这能为你带来什么？你认为"成功"能为你带来什么？你如何定义成功？这种定义从何而来？（00:13:30）  
在我的第一本书《重启》中，我讲述了自己追寻"柠檬糖"的历程。简而言之，我童年时期经历了巨大的混乱与不安——无论是经济上还是其他方面。而我生命中最大的稳定源泉是母亲的父母，我的祖父和祖母。祖父吉多是20世纪初从意大利南部移民来的冰贩子，总能从厨房外的绿色食品储藏室里拿出源源不断的柠檬糖。对我来说，稳定感和所谓的财富似乎与这种无限供应的柠檬糖紧密相连。  
到了30岁时，我表面上事业有成，身处风光无二的职场，但内心却毫无安全感，这让我陷入了深刻的反思。（00:15:02）  
所以我在《重启》中讲述这个故事，是为了探讨一个核心问题：金钱与我的职业选择、教育选择、安全感和自我价值感之间的关系是如何形成的。  
对你的问题我的长篇回复是，我鼓励人们问自己这类问题，从而提升自己的意识层级，让自己成为生活的掌控者，而不是延续童年时期为回应父母或祖父母焦虑而养成的刻板行为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a lot of people hearing this are afraid to ask these sorts of questions. The reason they don't ask these questions is because they worry that this is going to be like, okay, I got to quit my job, move to the woods, give up all these luxuries they have. I don't even want to think about that. I got a whole family to support. I got to succeed. Advice for getting over that hump of just like-
turns.zh: 我觉得很多听到这些话的人都不敢问这类问题。他们之所以不问，是因为担心这会导致——好吧，我得辞掉工作，搬到深山老林去，放弃所有现有的生活享受。我甚至都不敢想这些。我还有一大家子要养活，我必须成功。如何克服这种心理障碍呢？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: So let's just pause, Lenny. Okay, so what you're doing in this moment is empathetically imagining what may be going on for your listener, but the empathy is actually based on your own question because you invited me on the show, you knew I was going to get to this point. So I'm imagining that as you take this in, that thought stream shows up for you. "Jerry," says Lenny, "If I open up that closet, all the shit's going to fall out, and what am I going to do with it?" Does that resonate at all?
turns.zh: 那我们先暂停一下，莱尼。好的，你现在所做的，就是在同理心地设想听众可能面临的处境，但这种同理心实际上是基于你自己的经历——毕竟你邀请我来参加节目，就知道我会谈到这个话题。所以我想象，当你听到这些话时，你的脑海中会浮现出这样的思路：“杰瑞，如果我打开那个衣柜，里面的东西都会倾泻而出，那我该怎么办？”你能感同身受吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is why I was nervous to have you on this podcast. I knew what you-
turns.zh: 这就是我邀请你上节目时感到紧张的原因。我知道你——

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: So answer my question.
turns.zh: 所以请回答我的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't think it's that strong for me to be afraid of that because I've taken a different path already and gotten off the career ladder climbing treadmill. On the other hand, back to your original question, we talked about being busy. I'm very guilty of that. I'm constantly trying to do less, but constantly doing more, and my life is just very busy.
turns.zh: 对我来说，恐惧这种情况的程度没那么严重，因为我已经选择了另一条路，跳出了职业晋升的怪圈。不过回到你最初的问题，我们谈到忙碌。我自己也深有体会。我总想减少工作量，却又总是做得更多，生活实在太忙碌了。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Thank you for giving me more of that answer. And trust me, your listeners are going to appreciate you being fully there in just the way you were. So let's take a step back. The fear is, if I can reflect back to your original question, the fear is if I go there, I don't know what's going to happen as a consequence of that. If I pause and ask myself, is this relationship working out for me? I might end up leaving this relationship. If I pause and ask myself if this career isn't working for me, I might leave my career. (00:18:25): And the good news bad news is that's true. That is absolutely true. And if we look at some of the other observations we were making before like anxiety and depression, we have this belief system that if I pay no attention to the thing that I'm afraid of, it's somehow going to magically go away. If we pay no attention to the source of discomfort, it's somehow going to go away. And that's not actually how life works. More often than not, what we do is we respond to the source of challenge, whether it's a discomfort in our relationship, whether it's a discomfort in the way my life has unfolded. We respond to it by plasting over band-aids and sometimes they're relatively healthy, we become obsessed with working out, or sometimes they're unhealthy. We become obsessed with work or substance abuse or that kind of thing. Or sometimes, and this is super popular right now, we lean into what I would call as a spiritual bypassing where we go to Peru and we go do ayahuasca or we spend the weekend doing mushrooms with friends... (00:20:08): And what we're really not doing, Lenny, is confronting the parts of ourselves that need some tending to because we're afraid of the consequences. But I'll tell you a quick quote. One of my favorite books is Bruce Springsteen's autobiography, and about in the middle of the book, he has this passage where he talks about having spent 25 years in psychoanalysis. So let me just let that statement land. Bruce fucking Springsteen, 25 years in psychoanalysis. And he has this passage where he talks about the unsorted baggage of our childhood. And what he rightly asserts is that we all have unsorted baggage, and at some point we're going to pay the price of not sorting that baggage. And the price more often than not is in tears. (00:21:21): Now, this is Bruce Springsteen talking about this. This is not some airy-fairy transpersonal Jerry Colonna coach. And the reason I draw that out is we as children are socialized not to develop these consciousness skills. We are socialized to develop what I would call bypassing skills. And as he correctly points out, if you continue to bypass sorting out your baggage, there's going to come a day where you're going to have to pay that price. It could be in your own depression, it could be in, I've seen this a thousand times Lenny, entrepreneurs sabotaging their successful businesses because the belief system from their childhood goes something like, I don't deserve success so let me blow it up. We put this all under the rubric of midlife, but I don't know, when does midlife begin, 35? When does it end, 70? What I do know is it's the bulk of our adulthood.
turns.zh: 谢谢你能多给我一些这样的回答。相信我，你的听众会感激你能如此全身心投入地回答问题。那么让我们回过头来。恐惧在于，如果我回想起你最初的问题，恐惧在于如果我去面对它，我不知道会带来什么后果。如果我停下来问自己，这段关系对我来说是否行得通？我可能会选择离开这段关系。如果我停下来问自己，这份事业对我来说是否行不通？我可能会选择离开这份事业。（00:18:25）好消息坏消息是，这确实是事实。这绝对是事实。再看看我们之前提到的其他观察，比如焦虑和抑郁，我们有这样一种信念体系：如果我不去关注我害怕的东西，它就会神奇地消失。如果我们不去关注不适的根源，它就会神奇地消失。但生活并非如此。更多时候，我们会对挑战的根源做出反应，无论是关系中的不适，还是生活发展的不顺。我们通过贴创可贴来应对这些挑战，有时这些创可贴相对健康，比如沉迷于健身；有时则不健康，比如沉迷于工作或药物滥用……（00:20:08）而莱尼，我们真正没有做的，就是面对需要关注的自我部分，因为我们害怕其后果。但我要引用一句快餐式灵性绕开术：布鲁斯·斯普林斯汀在秘鲁服用死藤水，或是和朋友们周末吸食蘑菇……（00:21:21）现在，布鲁斯·斯普林斯汀在谈论这个。这可不是什么空想的跨个人派杰瑞·科洛纳教练。我强调这一点，是因为我们小时候被社会化成不去发展这些意识技能，而是发展所谓的绕开技能。正如他正确指出的那样，如果你继续绕开整理自己的行李，总有一天你会付出代价。这代价可能是抑郁，可能是……莱尼，我见过无数这样的例子，创业者因为童年信念系统而自毁成功的事业。比如“我不配成功，所以我要毁掉它”。我们把这一切都归结为中年危机，但我不知道，中年从何时开始，35岁？何时结束，70岁？但我知道，这构成了我们成年生活的大部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I think you've done an excellent job convincing me and others to spend time on this now, and I think there's an assumption of it gets harder, the tears get more intense as you wait longer. There's this ticking time bomb that better some amount of tears now than 10 times more tears later. Is that right?
turns.zh: 好的，我觉得你已经出色地说服了我和其他人现在就花时间讨论这个问题了。我觉得有一个假设是，随着时间推移，事情会越来越难，眼泪会越来越多。这就像一枚滴答作响的定时炸弹，现在流一点眼泪，总比以后流十倍的眼泪要好。这对吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well said.
turns.zh: 说得好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So coming back to this equation, I think I want to give people some things to do now that they may be likely convinced, okay, I should really rethink what I'm doing. So back to the equation, practical skills plus radical self-inquiry plus shared experiences equals enhanced leadership and greater resilience. So the three things you can work on are practical skills, radical self-inquiry, shared experiences, skills I think people get. So radical self-inquiry, these are essentially questions to dig into what drives you, what makes you happy. What are some questions again that people should be asking there as they're listening or maybe after they finish listening?
turns.zh: 好的。回到这个等式，我想现在我要给人们一些可以做的事情，让他们更有可能被说服，好，真的应该重新思考我正在做的事情。所以回到这个等式，实践技能加上深度自省再加上共同经历等于提升领导力和增强韧性。所以你可以努力提升的三个方面是实践技能、深度自省和共同经历，我认为这些技能是人们能够掌握的。那么深度自省，本质上就是挖掘驱动你、让你快乐的东西的那些问题。再问一下，在听讲座或者听完讲座后，人们应该问自己哪些问题呢？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: In the time since I've been a coach, which is now going on 27 years, the popularity of journaling has gone up, which is awesome. And part of what happens is people journal, but they don't know what they should be journaling or how they should. So let me give some questions then, and this is a way to approach it. Let's imagine that what we're trying to do, whether we're sitting in meditation, whether we're journaling, whether we're taking time away, we're just pausing and starting to ask ourselves questions. So my famous questions include things like, what am I not saying that I need to say? So let's imagine ourselves in a relationship that's not working. (00:24:30): Talk about something that could be terrifying. What am I not saying in that relationship that I need to say? By the way, this is a good question to ask if one is responsible for leading people too. Corollary questions to that would be, what am I saying that's not being heard? And then, of course, what's being said that I'm not hearing? So if we just pause and look at those four questions, how have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want? What am I not saying that I need to say? What am I saying that's not being heard? And what's being said that I'm not hearing? Can you feel the power of all of that in those questions?
turns.zh: 从我成为教练以来的这27年里，日记写作的流行程度越来越高，这很棒。其中一个问题是，人们写日记，但不知道该写什么或者怎么写。所以让我给出一些问题，作为一种方法。假设我们现在无论是坐着冥想，还是写日记，或者是抽空休息，开始问自己一些问题。所以我著名的几个问题包括，比如，我需要说出口但没说出口的话是什么？假设我们处在一段不顺利的关系中。（00:24:30）谈论一些可能令人恐惧的事情。我在那段关系中需要说出口但没说出口的话是什么？顺便说一句，如果你也负责领导他人，这也是个很好的问题。与此相关的其他问题包括，我说了但没被听到的话是什么？当然，还有，我没听到别人说了的话是什么？如果我们停下来看看这四个问题，我是如何参与创造了自己说不想拥有的条件的？我需要说出口但没说出口的话是什么？我说了但没被听到的话是什么？还有，我没听到别人说了的话是什么？你能感受到这些问题中的力量吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Scary questions.
turns.zh: 是的。令人恐惧的问题。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: They are scary questions. You know you're in the radical self-inquiry zone when the questions take your breath away, when the questions, and by the way, you don't have to share the answers to these questions with anybody but yourself. Now, there could be some power in sharing them in a group of friends and sharing them with a group of colleagues, sharing them with a coach, sharing them with a therapist. But the most important person with whom you should share the answers is oneself. This is a little bit of Buddhism here. Self-delusion along with attachment are the biggest contributors to our own suffering. Self-delusion. Everything's great. How you doing? Everything's great. Bullshit. Can we just not bullshit each other? (00:26:30): So let me just pause. Those are just four questions. My first book Reboot has a set of questions after every single chapter. We also have a journal that we put out that has questions and questions, but the more important thing to take away from this is questions that startle us, questions that may cause us to be a little afraid of the answer, that's where the gold is.
turns.zh: 它们确实是令人恐惧的问题。当这些问题让你屏息时，你就知道自己进入了深度自省的境界。顺便说一句，你不必把这些问题的答案分享给任何人，只需自己知晓即可。当然，在朋友小组中或与同事、教练、治疗师分享这些问题也可能很有力量。但最重要的是，你应该把答案分享给自己。这里有点佛教的意味。自欺和执着是我们自己痛苦的最大来源。自欺。一切都很好。你好吗？一切都很好。胡说八道。我们能不能别互相糊弄了？（00:26:30）所以让我暂停一下。这只是四个问题。我的第一本书《重启》在每一章后都附有一组问题。我们还出版了一本日志，里面也满是问题，但更重要的是，要记住那些让我们震惊的问题，那些可能让我们对答案感到有些害怕的问题，这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And we'll point people to the book for many more of these questions and the worksheets. For the third party equation, shared experiences, can you explain what that is?
turns.zh: 我们会引导人们去书中寻找更多这类问题和工作表。对于第三个等式中的共同经历，你能解释一下这是什么吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: We were talking about socialization, for example. Prior to launching Reboot, the company, my co-founder, Ali Schultz and I, the roots of Reboot the company began with me designing, or Ali and I designing these boot camps. And the original iteration of the boot camp, we used to call CEO Boot Camp because it was originally we would get first-time CEOs together and we would do a bait and switch. We would pretend to sell them practical skills, and then I would start asking really tough questions like who would you be without the story of who you are? It's like what? (00:27:57): The notion of shared experience as an important component grew out of that. Because what would happen is imagine sitting in a circle of people who just have your back, who really care about you as a person. And imagine then discussing some of the answers to those questions. Who would you be without the story of who you are? What is it that you wish that people in your life knew about you, but you're too afraid to tell them? And imagine sitting in a group of people who can just hold that space without fixing you, without telling you what you're doing right or wrong? We, too often than not, especially in what I would say the entrepreneurial community are socialized to bullshit not only ourselves, but everybody else. All our companies are moving up into the right, every product that's working, we don't really have any problems because we're crushing it, and that's just a lie. Imagine having the capacity to be in relationship with people where you can just tell the truth. That's what shared experiences are about.
turns.zh: 比如，我们之前谈到社交化。在创立Reboot之前，我和联合创始人阿里·舒尔茨（Ali Schultz）最初设计的CEO训练营项目，最初被称为"CEO训练营"。我们会把初次担任CEO的人聚集在一起，先假装向他们传授实用技能，然后我会抛出一些尖锐的问题，比如"如果没有你的个人故事，你会是谁？"这类问题。（00:27:57）：共享经验作为重要组成部分的理念就由此而来。因为想象一下，当你坐在一群全心支持你、真正关心你的人中间，讨论这些问题的答案会是怎样的——"如果没有你的个人故事，你会是谁？"你希望生活中的人了解你的哪些方面，却又不敢说出口？想象一下，当你身处一群能接纳你本真、不会评判你对错的人中间会是怎样的情景。我们太常被社会化了，尤其是创业圈的人，习惯对自己和他人撒谎。我们总说公司蒸蒸日上，产品大获成功，却这不过是自欺欺人。想象能与人坦诚相待的场景，这才是共享经验的意义所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My wife does a women's circle where they gather and just share what's really going on within in their lives. And it's-
turns.zh: 我妻子组织了一个女性圈子，她们聚在一起分享生活中的真实经历。这——

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: That's it.
turns.zh: 就是全部了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's very confidential. There's a ritual to it, and it feels like that's a really good avenue for things like that.
turns.zh: 而且非常保密。活动有特定的仪式感，感觉这是处理此类问题的绝佳途径。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: What circle do you sit in?
turns.zh: 你参加哪个圈子？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No circles. This is my circle.
turns.zh: 没有圈子。这就是我的圈子。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: But there is something powerful here. I think in the last 15 years, the rise of podcasts, good podcasts. What I think what happens is let's hope this is happening for your audience right now, good quality intimate conversation between people who are authentic and real, creates space for someone to be authentic and real, even if it's just with themselves. So you're doing a mitzvah, you're doing a good deed by creating this space.
turns.zh: 但这里有一种强大的力量。我认为过去15年，播客的兴起，特别是优质播客的兴起，让人们有了真诚交流的空间。希望你们的听众现在也能感受到这种氛围——真实、真诚的人们之间高质量的深度对话，为人们创造了一个能做真实自我的空间，哪怕只是对自己而言。这就是在行善，为他人创造这样的空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks, Jerry. Let's go back to the busyness point, and I'll talk about myself a bit to get it real again, because I think it's also something a lot of people struggle with. I listen to this, they're just like, I'm so busy, and every time someone ask me how I'm doing, busy, so busy, like swirly eyes emoji, swirly eyes emoji.
turns.zh: 谢谢，杰瑞。让我们回到忙碌这个话题，我再谈谈我自己，让话题更接地气，因为我觉得这也是很多人面临的困境。我听他们说，我太忙了，每次有人问我近况，我都回答忙，忙得晕头转向，眼睛都发花，眼睛都发花。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: With a little head shake.
turns.zh: 还摇摇头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. And the melting face emoji. And that's very much me. And it's funny because I started this journey of the newsletter of just like I call the project avoid getting a real job. And it was just like, cool, just do this newsletter thing, not have the job. It'll be chill, write an email once a week. But I just find myself taking on endlessly more and more. And for me, I feel like the drive is it's just fun to see it grow and for it to keep building and doing well. (00:31:17): This reminds me, there's a quote that Will Smith shared once that I think you'll like. Someone asked him what it's like to be famous, and he's like, "Really awesome as you're going up to fame. Pretty okay as a famous person. Really bad when you lose that fame." And that's how it feels with the growth of this thing. It's just like growth is up. Oh, life's good, and then it starts to stall. I'm like, oh, no, it's all going to fall apart. So I think that's where a lot of that comes from for me. It's just like, oh, what's next? I got to, let's see what else I can do here.
turns.zh: 没错。还有那个融化的脸表情符号。这太像我了。说起来挺有趣的，我当初开始做这个时事通讯项目时，就跟自己说"别去找份正经工作"。当时想着，挺酷的，就做这个通讯吧，不用工作多轻松，每周写封邮件就行。但后来我发现自己承担的任务越来越多。对我来说，动力就在于看着它不断发展壮大，看着它做得越来越好，这很有趣。（00:31:17）这让我想起威尔·史密斯曾说过的一句话，我觉得你会喜欢的。有人问他当名人是什么感觉，他说：“成名过程很棒。成名后还不错。但失去名气时就糟透了。”这就是这个项目发展历程的感觉。成长就是上升阶段，生活很美好，然后开始停滞。我就会想，哦，不，一切都要崩塌了。所以这就是我很多焦虑的根源。我就会想，接下来该做什么？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, how do you feel about yourself when you're on that growth trajectory?
turns.zh: 那在成长过程中，对自己的感觉如何？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel great.
turns.zh: 感觉很棒。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Say more.
turns.zh: 再详细说说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I'm achieving and heading in a... Part of it is just fun. It's like fun to win. So it's just like, yeah, we're doing it. It's working.
turns.zh: 我觉得自己在取得成就，朝着一个方向前进……其中一部分就是很有趣。胜利的感觉很棒。所以我们就坚持做下去，事情在往好的方向发展。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: And when you're not growing, how do you feel about yourself?
turns.zh: 那不成长的时候，自己又会怎么想？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: About myself. There's this sense that it's all over. Oh, maybe it's all going to fall apart, and maybe I'm not as good at this as I thought, and maybe-
turns.zh: 对自己而言。会有种一切都要结束的感觉。哦，也许一切都要崩塌了，也许我没自己想的那么擅长这个，也许——

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Okay, so stay in that spot for a moment. So imagine, and I don't know that this is true, but I can imagine that there's a little whispery voice in your head that's always there that says, "Lenny, you're not as good as you think you are. In fact, Lenny, they might even find out."
turns.zh: 好的，先在原地站一会儿。想象一下——我不知道这是否属实，但我能想象在你脑海里有个始终低声耳语的声音：“莱尼，你并没有自己想象中那么优秀。事实上，莱尼，他们可能会发现的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep. Yeah, imposter syndrome.
turns.zh: 没错。是啊，冒名顶替综合症。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Oh, shit. So by being busy and by being on that growth trajectory, that voice maybe sounds a little less persistent, maybe a little less loud. Now, I want to offer a different potential. What if you could enjoy the puzzle of trying to create something new, trying to create magic, something out of nothing, but it doesn't matter to your sense of self-esteem if you succeed or fail. What if what drove you was not quieting that voice, but what drove you was, oh, this is just fun? Seth Godin, who's a dear, dear friend of mine, talks about art projects.
turns.zh: 天哪。所以当你忙碌于事业，处于成长轨道时，这个声音或许会稍微弱一些，声音也可能稍微小一些。现在，我想提出一个不同的可能性。如果你能享受创造新事物的挑战，享受从无到有创造奇迹的过程，而无论成功与否都不会影响你的自尊心呢？如果驱使你的不是让那个声音安静下来，而是“这太有趣了”呢？我的好朋友赛斯·戈丁（Seth Godin）谈到过艺术项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also a former podcast guest.
turns.zh: 他也是我播客的嘉宾。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: So what if you just approached the project as if it was an art project? I think it's going to show up this way. What if it turns out it's wrong? What if it's this? What if it's that? And your sense of self-esteem is not attached to the outcome.
turns.zh: 那么，如果你把这个项目当作艺术项目来对待呢？我觉得结果会是这样的。如果结果证明是错的呢？如果是这样呢？如果是那样呢？而你的自尊心并不依附于最终结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting is that's how I started this whole thing. I had no intention of it being a career and way I make a living. It was just, this is cool, people seem to like it, I enjoy it. Let's just see where it goes. No expectations.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我就是这样开始这整个事业的。我从没想过要把它当作职业或谋生的手段。只是觉得这很酷，人们似乎喜欢它，我也乐在其中。看看它能发展到什么程度。没有任何期待。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: And then what happened?
turns.zh: 然后呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then it worked.
turns.zh: 然后它成功了。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: It became successful.
turns.zh: 它变得成功了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. It worked out.
turns.zh: 没错。事情进展得很顺利。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Right. It became successful, meaning you developed an audience, meaning you developed a following.
turns.zh: 对。它取得了成功，也就是说你积累了听众，意味着你赢得了追随者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, income. That was a big part of it.
turns.zh: 然后就是收入。这是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: And then you developed an income, and then the stakes went up, and then all of a sudden, my heart, the anxiety.
turns.zh: 接着你有了收入，压力随之而来，突然间，我的心情变得焦虑不安。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not quite that strongly. At times it is, but there's a bit of just, oh, wow, I am relying on this now. I can't just let it fall apart.
turns.zh: 倒也不至于那么强烈。有时确实会这样，但有时候也会想，哦，我现在得依赖这个了。我不能让它崩盘。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Because my life would fall apart if I let it fall apart.
turns.zh: 因为如果让它崩盘，我的整个生活都会崩盘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, life would change in a big way if this whole thing ends.
turns.zh: 是啊，如果这整件事结束了，生活会发生巨大的变化。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Right. Right. So what you're talking about, what we're talking about right now, remember before I said in Buddhism, we talk about self-delusion and attachment. Now, we're talking about attachment. When we become attached to the outcome, we inadvertently fuel our own suffering. When we become attached, and in this case, okay, I get it. There's a financial reality. This is important because it helps pay the bills, if it doesn't entirely pay the bills. Great. Got it. Fabulous. But really the deeper attachment is see, I'm not nothing. See, I'm not a nobody, I'm a somebody, and that's the source of the suffering.
turns.zh: 对。对。所以你现在谈论的，我们现在讨论的，记住我之前在佛教里说过的，我们谈论自欺和执着问题。现在我们谈论执着。当我们执着于结果时，我们无意中加剧了自己的痛苦。当我们执着时，比如说好吧，我懂了。有财务现实。这很重要，因为它能帮我们支付账单，如果不能完全支付账单的话。很好。我懂了。太棒了。但更深层的执着在于，看，我不是什么都不算。我不是无名小卒，我是个重要的人，而这正是痛苦的根源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so true. That is very much a part of what has driven me is I was always a very shy kid growing up, and I don't think people expected a lot of me except my mom and dad, I guess. And so, I always had the sense, I'll show them, I'll show them what I could do, and that's always, it's this chip on the shoulder thing that I know drives a lot of people.
turns.zh: 这太对了。这在很大程度上推动着我前进的动力。我从小就是个很害羞的孩子，我觉得除了我父母，别人对我没抱多大期望。所以我总有种感觉，我要让他们看看，我要向他们展示我的能力，而这种自负心理，我知道这驱使着很多人。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: How old are you, Lenny?
turns.zh: 伦尼，你多大了？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Okay. So maybe now at 43, you can take in the fact that you are somebody regardless of what you do. What's your wife's name?
turns.zh: 好吧。那么也许现在43岁的你能接受，无论你做什么，你都是重要的。你妻子叫什么名字？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Michelle.
turns.zh: 米歇尔。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Is she going to love you even if the podcast fails?
turns.zh: 即使播客失败了，她也会爱你吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: What, is she an idiot? No, she's a smart person. The people who actually know you and care about you may be proud of your efforts, but their love for you is not dependent upon its success. And that's like a rewiring. Do you have children?
turns.zh: 什么，她是傻瓜吗？不，她是个聪明人。真正了解你、关心你的人可能会为你的努力感到骄傲，但他们的爱并不取决于你的成功。这就像重新建立连接。你有孩子吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we got a 22-month-old now.
turns.zh: 有，我们现在有个22个月大的孩子。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Oh, mazel tov. That's wonderful. My children are 34, 32, and 28. So I'll speak like the old man that I am. When we take that test, that spelling test, and we stick it with magnets on the refrigerator, it's at a pride. The challenging message that we inadvertently can send to our children is that we only love them because they got an A on the spelling test. And so, it's really critically important that we as parents do our own internal work to convey that unconditional love that is our birthright as human beings. And we hold onto the goal because the goal is cool, because solving a puzzle is fun, because doing hard work and experiencing the reward from that is affirming, but your value as a human being is unshakable. Now, as a father, isn't that the feeling you want your child to have?
turns.zh: 哦，恭喜你啊！太棒了。我的孩子们分别34岁、32岁和28岁。所以让我以一个过来人的身份来分享心得。当我们把拼写测试卷用磁铁贴在冰箱上时，那确实是一种自豪感。但我们无意中传递给孩子的信息可能是：我们只爱他们是因为他们拼写测试得了A。所以作为父母，我们必须进行自我反思，传递出那种与生俱来的无条件的爱。我们的价值是不可动摇的。现在，作为父亲，难道这不是你希望孩子拥有的感觉吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And there's a lot of parenting advice these days that helps you learn to do that. There's all these TikToks now, don't say good job. Just say good choice or great, hard work. Great job working hard on that.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。如今有很多育儿建议能帮助我们做到这一点。比如TikTok上的视频，别说“干得好”，而要说“选得好”或者“棒极了”，还有“辛苦了”之类的。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Right, right, right. I don't know how I feel about getting parenting advice from TikTok, but okay.
turns.zh: 对对对。我不知道从TikTok上获取育儿建议是否靠谱，但还是可以接受的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to have Andrew Luo joining us today. Andrew is CEO of OneSchema, one of our longtime podcast sponsors. Welcome, Andrew.
turns.zh: 今天很高兴邀请到罗安德（Andrew Luo）加入我们。安德鲁是OneSchema的CEO，也是我们长期的播客赞助商之一。欢迎你，安德鲁。

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请，莱尼。很高兴能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is new with OneSchema, I know that you work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp and Vanta and Watershed. I heard you guys launch a new data intake product that automates the hours of manual work that teams spent importing and mapping and integrating CSV and Excel files.
turns.zh: 那么OneSchema有什么新动态吗？我知道你和Ramp、Vanta、Watershed等我最喜欢的公司合作过。我听说你们推出了一个新的数据接收产品，可以自动化团队导入和映射CSV、Excel文件所耗费的数小时手动工作。

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Yes. So we just launched the 2.0 of OneSchema file feeds. We've rebuilt it from the ground up with AI. We saw so many customers coming to us with teams of data engineers that struggled with the manual work required to clean messy spreadsheets. FileFeeds 2.0 allows non-technical teams to automate the process of transforming CSV and Excel files with just a simple prompt. We support all of the trickiest file integrations, SFTP, S3, and even email.
turns.zh: 是的。我们刚刚推出了OneSchema文件馈送2.0版本。我们从头到尾用AI重新构建了它。我们发现很多客户带着数据工程师团队来找我们，他们在清理混乱的电子表格时遇到了巨大的挑战。FileFeeds 2.0让非技术团队只需一个简单的提示，就能自动化CSV和Excel文件的转换过程。我们支持所有最棘手的文件集成，包括SFTP、S3，甚至电子邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to take this off our roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema?
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，如果我的团队要开发这样的集成功能，能把这项工作从路线图中移除，改用OneSchema不是很棒吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Luo
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of outages from even just a single bad record in transactions, employee files, purchase orders, you name it. Debugging these issues is often like finding a needle in a haystack. OneSchema stops any bad data from entering your system and automatically validates your files, generating error reports with the exact issues in all bad files.
turns.zh: 完全赞同，莱尼。我们听过太多因为交易、员工档案、采购订单中哪怕只有一条错误记录导致系统崩溃的恐怖故事。调试这些问题往往就像大海捞针一样困难。OneSchema能阻止任何错误数据进入你的系统，并自动验证你的文件，为所有错误文件生成带有精确问题的错误报告。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Andrew, thank you so much for joining me. If you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co. That's oneschema.co. (00:40:46): Just to close loop on this, I think as people hear this, I feel like, okay, cool, everything falls apart. Sure, my parents will love me, my wife will love me, they won't think less of me. However, it's nice to get that really nice couch and that nice hotel and the income, the comfort that comes with income at a certain level is hard to give up. How do you help people get past that that might go away and feel comfortable?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会给客户带来各种困扰，还会迅速丧失他们的信任。安德鲁，非常感谢你参与访谈。如果你想了解更多信息，可以访问oneschema.co。就是oneschema.co。（00:40:46）：最后再总结一下。我觉得听完这些，人们可能会想，嗯，挺好的，一切都崩塌了。当然，父母会爱我，妻子也会爱我，他们不会看不起我。然而，拥有一张舒适的沙发、入住豪华酒店，以及获得一定收入所带来的安稳感，这些都让人难以割舍。当这些可能消失时，怎样才能帮助人们克服这种恐惧，重新获得安心呢？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, the good news is, and again, this is a Buddhist reference. The good news is there's a wisdom tradition that teaches all about this. So very briefly, the Buddhist story is in his mid-30s, he wakes up to the truth of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Birth, old age, sickness and death. And he wanders into the forest and he becomes a wandering mendicant and he becomes a holy man, and he's still not satisfied. And as I like to tell the story, one day he decides, fuck it, I'm just going to sit under the Bodhi tree and I'm not going to move until I figure this shit out. And so, he sits and sits and sits, and the story is he sat for 40 days living on a single grain of rice every day because always right, crazy stuff. (00:42:05): And when he woke up, he woke up to the four noble truths and the four noble truths are life is filled with suffering, that which we do to push away suffering increases suffering. The third noble truth is that there's an end to suffering. That's a really important one. And the fourth noble truth is what's known as the eightfold path to the end of suffering. (00:42:34): So let's focus on the second noble truth because that's really what you're talking about. When we acquire that nice couch, when we buy that nice house that stretches our income to its maximum, if we're doing it to enjoy the couch or the house, then A-OK. But if we're doing it because we're trying to push away the suffering of am I good enough to be loved, to feel safe, and that I belong, that which we do to push away suffering will increase suffering. And in this case, oh my God, what if they take my house away from me? Oh my God, what if I fall backwards down that staircase of life? Oh my God, what if all of those people who have signed up to my Substack suddenly disappear? You see how the attachment becomes that source of suffering? You see how the thing that we do to make ourselves feel better in fact fuels the tenuous hold that we have on our OK-ness? I'm okay just as I am. I'm okay. (00:44:03): It all comes down to why we're doing what we're doing. Now, to be clear, this is hard for me. I think it's hard for everybody. When my first book came out, Dan Harris, who's a really good friend and client from 10% Happier said to me, "Don't read the Amazon reviews." The truth is, I've read two reviews. I read it in the first hour after it was released, and I've never read a review since because there's no way I can experience those reviews without becoming attached to how people feel. So thank you. I'll put it over here and I'll just stay focused on the experience that I get from writing. (00:45:04): And yes, do I want to sell thousands of books? Do I want people to feel moved by my writing? I do, but you know who gets the most out of my writing? Me, because when I sit down, this is my file folder for whatever I might do for our next book, what I'm trying to do is answer questions that I have. For example, Captain Chaos is running the country right now. What is it that the world is going to need two or three years from now? And what's my contribution to that world? Now, just as I say that, how does that feel to you? It's kind of settling. So I know that in order for me to feel good about my existence on this planet, I have to ask myself these questions and I have to attempt to answer these questions. Whether it turns into a book that people buy or not is secondary, I have to do this work regardless.
turns.zh: 嗯，好消息是——再说一次，这是佛教的典故。好消息是，有一种智慧传统可以为我们解答这一切。简单来说，佛陀的故事是这样的：他30多岁时，在梦醒后领悟了生、老、病、死的真相。生、老、病、死。然后他逃入森林，成为一个云游的乞丐，最终成为圣人。但他仍不满足。正如我常讲的故事，有一天他决定：去他的，我就坐在菩提树下，一动不动直到想通这一切。于是他日复一日地坐着，据说有40天每天只吃一粒米饭——真是疯狂至极。（00:42:05）当他醒来时，领悟了四圣谛：生命充满苦难，我们为逃避苦难而做的事反而加剧了苦难。第三圣谛是苦难终有尽头。这一点至关重要。第四圣谛是八正道，以此终结苦难。（00:42:34）但我们今天重点讨论第二圣谛，因为这正是你们所关心的核心。当我们买下那张漂亮沙发，或是买下那栋耗尽我们收入极限的豪宅时，如果是为了享受沙发或房子的舒适，那没问题。但如果是为了逃避“我不够好，不值得被爱、缺乏安全感、被边缘化”的苦难，那么我们为逃避苦难所做的努力，反而会加剧苦难。例如：如果他们夺走我的房子怎么办？如果我从楼梯上摔下去怎么办？如果订阅我的Substack的人突然消失怎么办？你看，这种执着如何成为苦难的根源？你看，我们为了自我安慰所做的努力，如何反倒巩固了我们对“我还不错”的脆弱信念？我本就足够好，我本就没问题。（00:44:03）归根结底，关键在于我们为何要做我们正在做的事。说实话，这对我来说很难。对每个人来说都很难。我的第一本书出版时，《10%更快乐》的丹·哈里斯对我说：“别看亚马逊评论。”说实话，我只看了两条评论。书刚发布的第一个小时看了一条，此后再没看过，因为看到那些评论我会执着于别人的看法。所以谢谢你们。我把这事放在一边，专注于写作带来的体验。（00:45:04）是的，我希望卖出几千本书吗？我希望人们被我的文字感动吗？我确实希望，但你们知道谁从中收获最多吗？是我自己。因为当我坐下来写作时，这就是我为下一本书准备的文件夹，我试图回答自己的问题。比如，“混乱之王”现在执掌大局。未来两三年世界需要什么？我能为这个世界贡献什么？就在我说出这句话时，你们有什么感受？这种感觉很踏实。所以我知道，要想在地球上安心生活，我必须自问这些问题，并努力寻找答案。至于书能否畅销，那是次要的，无论如何我都要做这份工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That super connects with exactly again, the way I started this whole thing is I started writing just to crystallize my own thinking, and it ends up being useful to other people.
turns.zh: 这再次与我的初衷完美契合——我最初开始写作，纯粹是为了理清自己的思路，最终却对他人有所启发。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People hear this and they're like, why would I want to give up this great couch and house and car and all these things? That's really hard. And risking that by just doing something that feels good versus it'll make income, but it actually works. That's what I found. If you focus on a thing that is useful to yourself and interesting and not come at it from how do I make the most amount of money and turn this into whole thing, but more just, this is really interesting. I'm going to see where this goes. It will work for me.
turns.zh: 人们听到这话会问：为什么要放弃这么好的沙发、房子，甚至汽车？这太难了。而去冒险追随内心的热爱，却未必能赚钱，但事实证明确实有效。这就是我的发现。如果你专注于对自己有用且感兴趣的事物，而不是一心想着如何赚最多钱，把这件事当作爱好而非事业，那么一切都会顺其自然。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Lenny, you implicitly asked a how question a few minutes ago. How do I do this? How do I do this radical self-inquiry? And I asked, I responded by offering a few questions. Let's build upon that for a moment, because what you are articulating right now is in the process of asking those questions, you can go back to what Simon Sinek would say is your why. You could go back to your core principle. You could go back to the centerpiece within you, which is what do I believe to be true about the world and how do I want to be in that world? You know what animates me right now is a question? With my children being fully fledged adults, I am really focused on what kind of ancestor to my descendants would I like to be? 20 years from now, 30 years from now, 40 years from now, I'll be gone. What would I like those who follow after me to believe to be true about me? (00:48:11): And you just paused. I can tell from the Adam's apple jumping up and down, that that question landed for you. It's a question of legacy. It's a question of meaning and purpose. At the end of my days, this is a question in Reboot, at the end of my days, what would I like the people who come after me to say about me? And what I want people to say about me is that he gave a shit about the world, he cared, and he tried, and he was kind. Those are the things that matter to me.
turns.zh: 莱尼，几分钟前你隐晦地提了一个问题。如何做到这一点？如何进行这种彻底的自我探索？我当时给出了几个问题，现在我们可以再深挖一下。你现在所阐述的正是这个过程——你可以追溯到西蒙·斯涅克所说的"为什么"。回归你的核心信念，回归你内心深处的信念——你如何看待这个世界，以及你想如何融入这个世界？现在激励我的，是一个问题：我的孩子们都已成年，我现在专注于——20年后，30年后，40年后，我离开这个世界时，我希望后人如何看待我？（00:48:11）你刚停顿了一下。从喉结上下起伏的动作可以看出，这个问题触动了你。这关乎遗产，关乎意义与目标。生命即将结束时，我在Reboot项目中思考——我希望后人如何评价我？我希望他们说：他关心这个世界，他尽力了，他善良。这些才是对我最重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm always reminded of that frame of reference when I go to a funeral and people reading the eulogy and the old advice of what do you want your eulogy to say and making that your mission. But on the flip side, there's this viral video of Mike Tyson. Someone was coming up to him I think before his big match recently, and asked him about his legacy, and he's like, "I don't give a shit about my legacy. It's just a made up thing that doesn't matter." So let me just ask you this. Why is it important to think about legacy? Does legacy even matter? We're dead. What's the difference?
turns.zh: 每当参加葬礼，听人们宣读悼词，回想“你希望自己的悼词如何？”这种古老的忠告，并以此为人生使命时，我总会想起这个参照系。但另一方面，网上有个关于迈克·泰森的视频。最近在他大赛前，有人问他对遗产的看法，他回答：“我才不在乎遗产呢，那不过是虚构的概念，无关紧要。”所以我要问你：为什么思考遗产很重要？遗产真的重要吗？我们终将死去，有什么区别呢？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Far be it for me to criticize Mike, and don't hit me Mike, because even as an old guy, I wouldn't want to be hit by Mike Tyson. I don't know what's behind his response, but I can tell you what's true for me. I made oblique reference to Captain Chaos in the world as it is right now. The world's a tough place right now. We live in a world where it's almost normalized that a teenager will shoot other teenagers in school. It's almost normalized that people are dragged off to jail. Something is happening, something that's really disturbing. (00:50:28): Now, to be clear, we've always had disturbing times. I mean, I was reminded recently, I'm reading a book called Soldiers and Kings, which I highly recommend, which is about human smuggling from Central America into the United States, and it's an extraordinary book. And in reading that, I was reminded of policies that the US government has used over the years, whether it's supporting dictators in Central America or other sorts of things, things that I oppose, that feel immoral, if not directly immoral. (00:51:15): Why does this come up for me? I can't shake the feeling that someone down the line in my lineage is going to ask of me, "And what did you do, grandpa? And what did you do, great grandpa?" I know what I want that answer to be, which is I tried. Lenny, God gave me the ability to put two sentences together in a way that people listen. I feel a moral responsibility to use that God-given gift to help create the world, that I would like to see, a world of kindness and empathy, a world where poverty is diminished, a world where people feel safe however the fuck they identify. I don't give a damn. So is that my legacy? Yeah, and maybe there's some ego implicit in that, but can I go on for just a bit on this?
turns.zh: 我绝不是要批评迈克，迈克别打我啊，因为即便我是个老头子，也不想被迈克·泰森揍。我不知道他回应背后的原因，但我可以说说我自己的看法。我含糊地提到了当下世界的混乱局面。当前世界局势确实严峻。如今青少年在校园里开枪袭击同龄人几乎成了常态，人们被拖进监狱也屡见不鲜。某些事情正在发生，而这些事着实令人不安。（00:50:28）当然，世界从来都不平静。最近我读了一本叫《士兵与国王》的书，强烈推荐这本讲述中美洲人口走私的著作，内容极其震撼。读这本书时，我联想到美国政府多年来推行的政策——无论是支持中美洲独裁者，还是其他种种我反对的、甚至感觉不道德的行径。（00:51:15）为什么我会想起这些？我总挥之不去的疑问是：将来我的后代会问我：“爷爷，你做了什么？曾祖父，你又做了什么？” 我希望自己的回答是：我尽力了。莱尼，上帝赋予我用两句话让人们倾听的能力。我觉得有道德责任利用这份天赋，帮助创造一个我向往的世界——一个充满善意和同理心的世界，一个贫困减少的世界，一个人们无论以何种身份都能感到安全的世界。我不在乎别人怎么看。这会是我的遗产吗？是的，或许这里面有自负的成分，但能否让我再多说几句？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然可以。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: At the end of Reboot, I write about this moment, and in this moment I am in Marin County. My wife Allie and I are together. And I'm once again torturing myself with this question. Have I been a good man? I drive myself crazy with that question. Have I been a good father? Have I been a good partner? Have I been a good man? And she says, in a very frustrated way, "All right, already. Enough. You're a good man. Stop." And so, I go for a walk, and as I'm walking, I encounter this toppled over oak tree and the roots are all torn up and you've seen trees like this, and clearly the tree died and clearly a wind came and clearly knocked the whole thing down. And I look at the tree and I say to myself, "Here lies a good man." (00:53:57): And I liken myself to this toppled over oak tree, and I imagine that that tree had lived its life with its limbs gnarled and twisted by actions that it should have taken and actions that it shouldn't have taken, but good choices and bad choices. But that for the majority of its 75, 80 years, it lived into its purpose of providing shelter and shade for those that may have come from beneath it. And I make this point that at the end of my days, I want to be like this tree just slowly dissolving into the earth, having done the best job I could of being purposeful. I feel better. My suffering is eased when I can lean into that, which then makes me able to be present for the other person, whether it's a coaching client, whether it's a podcast conversation, whether it's just going for a walk with one of my children. I just feel better, and I think I am a better person when I think about things like that. So far be it from me to disagree with Mike Tyson, but I think he's wrong.
turns.zh: 重启之旅的结尾，我写下了那一刻。在那一刻，我身处马林县。我的妻子艾莉和我在一起。我又一次用这个问题折磨自己：我是个好人吗？我被这个问题折磨得快疯了。我是个好父亲吗？我是个好伴侣吗？我是个好人吗？她很不耐烦地说：“好吧，就这样，够了。你是个好人。别问了。” 于是，我出去散步。走着走着，我遇到了那棵被连根拔起的橡树。你见过这样的树，显然它已经死去，被狂风刮倒了。我看着那棵树，心里默念：“这里躺着一个好人。” （00:53:57） 我把自己比作这棵被连根拔起的橡树，想象它在75、80年的生命里，为可能从它树荫下走过的人遮风挡雨。它的大部分时间都在履行提供庇护和阴凉的使命。我想说的是，在我生命的尽头，我希望自己能像这棵树一样慢慢融入大地，用尽全力去实现自己的价值。这让我感觉好多了。当我专注于这些想法时，痛苦就减轻了。无论是与客户沟通，参与播客对谈，还是陪孩子们散步，我都能更好地投入当下。思考这些问题让我觉得自己是个更好的人。我绝无意反驳迈克·泰森的观点，但我认为他错了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good callback. It sounds like The Giving Tree to me.
turns.zh: 不错的联想。这让我想起了《给树的礼物》。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Oh, yes, yes. Shel Silverstein.
turns.zh: 哦，对，对。雪儿·西尔弗斯坦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give people something to do with this area of legacy. How did you approach coming up with figuring out what you wanted your legacy to be? Are there some questions you asked? Is there something you recommend folks do to help think through this for themselves?
turns.zh: 为了让人们对遗产这个话题有所启发。你是如何思考并确定自己希望留下的遗产的？你有没有提出过什么问题？有没有什么建议能帮助人们自己思考这个问题？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, it's delightful that we've ended up here because I think that I'm still working through those questions. As I said before as we both connected with, I use my writing to find my way to answers to questions. So part of what I'm dealing with right now is, look, I'll turn 62 this year. That feels old, but it also feels settled. And part of what I'm trying to figure out is what do I want my elderhood to be like? And I'll be honest, I'm enjoying this time of my life where I'm finding myself being a voice of comfort, being a voice of maybe even sanity in a time where that feels really insane and challenging. So maybe that's what my legacy will be. I'm not 100% sure.
turns.zh: 很高兴我们能聊到这儿，因为我觉得自己还在思考这些问题。正如我们之前提到的，我通过写作来寻找问题的答案。目前我面临的部分挑战是，今年我就要62岁了。这感觉很老，但也很安定。我想弄清楚的是，我希望自己的晚年生活是怎样的？说实话，我很享受现在的生活状态——我发现自己能成为一种安慰的声音，甚至在人们觉得疯狂和充满挑战的时刻，提供一份理智的声音。所以也许这就是我的遗产。我还不是百分之百确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is this maybe hinted the new book you're working on? Is this the topic you're thinking about or is this not?
turns.zh: 这或许暗示了你正在创作的新书？这是你正在思考的主题吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Yeah, and other things. That's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 是的，还有其他方面。没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of the world being very crazy right now, you talked about your kids, AI is very top of mind for a lot of people in particular. It's stressing a lot of people out. In a lot of ways, it's quite unsettling in future careers, in skills, people-
turns.zh: 说到当下世界非常疯狂，你提到了你的孩子们。人工智能尤其让很多人焦虑。它让很多人感到压力重重。在未来的职业生涯、技能方面——

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: It is unsettling, isn't it?
turns.zh: 这确实令人不安，不是吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Quite unsettling, but there's a world where we don't need humans in the future, potentially. Just what advice do you share with clients to help them work through this period of worry with the future, with AI being the core of it?
turns.zh: 确实令人不安，但未来或许真的无需人类存在。那么，您会给客户提供哪些建议，帮助他们度过这段对未来感到担忧的时期，而人工智能正是核心所在？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, if we go back to the equation for a moment, I think it's really important that we actually talk about these things. I would say a year ago, I likened it to the experience that I had. Remember, I'm old enough to remember when not everything had an IP address. Now, our refrigerators have IP addresses. I mean, it's freaking crazy. I'm old enough to remember when you had to install an IP stack into your personal computer in order to connect to the web. That's how old I am.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果我们暂时回归到这个问题上，我认为真正重要的是我们必须谈论这些事情。一年前，我曾将自己的经历与此相提并论。记住，我年纪足够大，记得那时并非所有设备都有IP地址。如今，我们的冰箱都有IP地址了。说真的，这简直太不可思议了。我还记得那时要在个人电脑上安装IP堆栈才能连接到网络。这足以说明我有多老了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you have the phone modem where you had to put the phone?
turns.zh: 你说的是需要把手机插到调制解调器上的那种吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Absolutely. Absolutely. It was a big, big deal to go from 1,200 baud to 2,400 baud to 56K. Oh my God, it was like a rocket ship. A year ago, I thought we were going through a similar kind of transition. We're clearly not. This is different. And in the coaching therapeutic world, everybody's like, "Oh my God, ChatGPT is going to replace me." And I don't know, maybe. What I am finding is... I wear glasses. So for those of you who are only listening to the audio, you may find that news. What I am finding is in my own life, it's like I have put on a pair of glasses that are really, really sharp and helpful, and it is disturbing and unsettling because I think it does challenge this question of what is our role as human beings? (00:59:46): Now, what I come back to, and I could be wrong, but what I come back to is we're talking through a medium, a mediated experience. My signal is bouncing up into the sky and to a satellite. I won't name the company, it's coming back down. I don't know what your access is. We're using this platform or a site to record this, but somehow we're still finding the capacity to be present for one another in a heart-to-heart way. (01:00:30): And so, when I look at these phenomena, what I lift up is that. What I am hopeful about is that that which does not matter in the experience of being human gets burned away and is taken care of, call it by AI, but that that which matters, which is presence and connection, human-to-human contact, strategic thinking, formulation, you want to talk about it in terms of engineering, the conceptualization, that that gets elevated and our skills get better at doing that. And in the most optimistic point of view, what ends up happening is we spend more time on that which matters, and less time on that which doesn't matter. And I could be completely wrong and we could all be out of work and making sure that the robots are well-oiled, and that becomes our purpose.
turns.zh: 没错，绝对是。速度从1200 baud提升到2400 baud，再到56K，这可是个巨大的进步。天哪，那感觉就像火箭般飞速前进。一年前，我以为我们正在经历类似的转变。但显然并非如此。这次情况不同。在心理辅导领域，每个人都在说：“天哪，ChatGPT要取代我们了。”我不知道，也许吧。但我发现……我戴眼镜了。所以对于只听音频的听众来说，这可能是个新闻。我发现，在我自己的生活中，我仿佛戴上了一副非常清晰且有用的眼镜，这确实令人不安和不安，因为我认为这确实挑战了我们作为人类的角色问题。（00:59:46）：现在，我回归到我的观点，可能我错了，但我认为我们是通过一种媒介、一种中介体验进行交流的。我的信号被传送到天空，传送到卫星。我不会说出公司的名字，它会传回来。不知道你们的网络情况如何。我们使用这个平台或网站来录制这个对话，但不知怎的，我们仍然能以心连心的方式相互陪伴。（01:00:30）：所以，当我观察这些现象时，我所强调的是：我所期待的是，在人类体验中无关紧要的东西会被淘汰掉，由人工智能处理，而真正重要的东西——比如存在感、人际联系、人与人之间的互动、战略思考、规划——你若从工程角度来看，就是概念化——这些会得到提升，我们在这方面的能力也会提高。从最乐观的角度来看，最终结果是我们会花更多时间在重要的事情上，而在无关紧要的事情上花更少时间。当然，我也可能完全错了，我们可能都失业了，只管确保机器人运转良好，这就成了我们的使命。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines of glasses and even coaching, the world of coaching, there's a really interesting use case I saw today that Dan Shipper shared that I think you'd love, which is now that ChatGPT has memory, remembers everything you've said, and you can think back, you can ask it, "What are blank spots in the way I see the world that I'm not seeing?" You could also upload all your chat transcripts from your meetings and ask it what could you do better in meetings?
turns.zh: 沿着眼镜甚至心理辅导的思路，我今天看到了丹·希珀分享的一个非常有趣的案例，我想你会喜欢的。那就是现在ChatGPT有了记忆功能，能记住你说过的所有内容，你可以回想起来，你可以问它：“在我的世界观中，有哪些空白点是我没有注意到的？”你还可以上传所有会议的聊天记录，问它在会议中可以做得更好的地方。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Look, one of my colleagues in the coaching company, he has uploaded, he kept all of his journal entries, I think over 10 years journal entries from Evernote, and he uploaded that. I think he uses Claude, and he's asked Claude to highlight things. What am I not saying that I need to say? What am I saying that's not being heard? He's asked it to reflect back, and I think it's been incredibly helpful for him. I think the result is that he is a better coach, which is interesting, because the feeling is, well, does this replace it? I am finding, I'm using ChatGPT really as a writing and thinking partner in a way that I did not have before, and I'm still using my live real human writing buddies, which are really important to me. Where does this all end up? I had no idea. It is unsettling, it's uncanny, and it's also enlivening and exciting.
turns.zh: 听着，我在教练公司的同事上传了自己十多年来在Evernote上记录的日志条目，还用Claude把内容进行了标注。他还让Claude反馈自己的表现，我觉得这真的很有帮助。结果是，他现在成为了一名更出色的教练。这挺有意思的，因为人们总会问，Claude会不会取代人类教练？但我发现，我现在把ChatGPT当作写作和思考的伙伴，这种体验前所未有，同时我依然会和现实中的写作伙伴保持联系，他们对我来说非常重要。这一切最终会走向何方？我现在也说不清。这既令人不安，又令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well put. I love that you can ask these hard questions of Claude/ChatGPT, these questions that make you really scared could ask it what are the answers, and even not have to do the hard work and maybe get a better answer. I doubt that that will give you the best answers.
turns.zh: 说得好。我很欣赏你能向Claude/ChatGPT提出这些尖锐的问题——这些问题会让你担心，生怕它给出错误答案，但你甚至不必自己费力思考，或许还能得到更优的答案。不过我怀疑这并不能给出最理想的答案。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, what it might do, which I think would be wonderful, is it might give you more questions to ask yourself. I'm a huge fan of powerful questions and the answer I give to a question like what am I not saying that I need to say? That question, you can ask yourself that question every single day. The question of how have I been complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want? You can ask yourself that question every single day. To take a step back, the subtitle of my first book is Leadership in the Art of Growing Up. The Art of Growing Up is a practice. It's not a scientific moment where one day you wake up and you're done. It's an ongoing practice of not continuous improvement, but continuous inquiry that can feel exhausting when you contemplate it, but enlivening when you live it.
turns.zh: 嗯，它或许能做到的，我觉得这会很棒，那就是能给你更多自我反思的机会。我特别推崇有力的提问。比如“我有什么没说出口的真心话？”这样的问题，你每天都可以问问自己。还有“我在哪些方面助长了自己所厌恶的现状？”这样的问题，也能每天自省。退一步说，我第一本书的副标题是《成长的艺术：领导力修行记》。成长的艺术是一种修行，不是某个科学时刻的顿悟，不是某天醒来就大功告成的。这是一种持续的修行，不是追求进步，而是持续探索。想想看，这听起来很累，但真正践行起来却充满生机。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All this, some people may think of as this whole idea of growth mindset. I know that you're not a big fan of this term, that it's used in a harmful way a lot of times. Can you just talk about that why you find that growth mindset as a concept isn't necessarily useful?
turns.zh: 所有这些，或许有人会把它归为成长型思维模式。我知道你不太喜欢这个术语，觉得它常被误用。你能谈谈为什么觉得成长型思维模式这个概念未必有用吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Here's what I have a problem with. First of all, having a growth mindset is a very, very helpful thing. What I have a problem is in having and how we can turn a notion like a growth mindset into a fixed mindset, which is, it's this funny little trick the ego does, and the ego says, "Okay, well, this is a growth mindset. Oh, this is not a growth mindset. Okay, then this is good. This is not good. This is bad. This is..." What Buddhism has taught me is that everything's falling apart all the time even our growth mindset. When we get too fixed on the proper way to do things, we're setting ourselves up for attachment and therefore suffering. So if you can hold something like a mindset loosely with that attachment, go for it. Have a blast. Enjoy it. But the minute you start to nail it down to the floor and say this is the way it ought to be, I ought to always have a growth mindset, you've become fixed. And that's what the ego does. (01:06:48): To be more explicit about it from a business context for example, the great business writer Peter Senge says, "It is virtually impossible to challenge the assumptions that made you rich in the first place." So think about it in our experience of starting a business. We have what the Zen Buddhist would say, beginner's mind, all things are possible. And then, we experience, you were talking about it a little before, a little bit of success, and the ego, which is so terrified of not having success, start to say, "Aha, this is the way to do it." And then, we start to deviate from that because life happens and then the anxiety starts. So the question is, how do you hold a growth mindset loosely knowing that you ought to stay present to the world as it is, respond to the changing dynamics, figure out what's next because that's the growth. So put succinctly, stay attached to the growth and hold mindset a little loosely.
turns.zh: 以下是我的疑惑所在。首先，拥有成长型思维模式确实非常有益。但让我不解的是，人们如何将成长型思维转化为固定型思维模式。这简直是自我意识的把戏——它会说：“好吧，这就是成长型思维。哦，这不是成长型思维。好，那样好。这不好……” 佛教教会我的一点是，一切都在不断崩塌，甚至包括我们的成长型思维。当我们过于执着于正确的做事方式时，就陷入了执着的陷阱，从而陷入痛苦。所以，如果你能以不执着的心态对待思维模式，那就尽情享受。但一旦你开始把它定死成“就该是这样”，你就陷入了固定思维模式。这正是自我意识的把戏。（01:06:48）：以商业语境为例，商业作家彼得·圣吉曾说：“要挑战那些最初让你致富的假设，几乎是不可能的。” 以我们创业的经验来说，佛教禅宗所说的初心——一切皆有可能。然后，当我们取得一点成功（你之前提到的）时，自我意识会说：“啊，这就是正确的做法。” 接着，我们会偏离正轨，因为生活本就无常，焦虑随之而来。所以问题在于，如何以不执着的心态保持成长型思维，知道自己应该顺应世界的变化，顺势而为，迎接下一个挑战，因为这才是成长的意义。简而言之，保持对成长的执着，同时对思维模式保持适度灵活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It reminds me of advice. I did a meditation retreat once, and there's always a sense with Buddhism, and it's interesting how often Buddhism and advice from Buddhist teachings comes up on this podcast by the way.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这番见解了。这让我想起佛教的教诲。顺便说一句，我曾参加过一次冥想静修，佛教总有一种智慧，而佛教教义和建议在这个播客中频频出现，确实很有趣。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: When the student is ready, the teacher will appear. You are inviting it in, but keep going.
turns.zh: 当学生准备好时，老师就会出现。你在主动吸引它，但请继续前行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense as you say that. Interesting. So there's this fear I think people have with Buddhist teachings that you will not be as ambitious and you will not achieve as much if you're not attaching.
turns.zh: 你说得对，这很合理。有趣的是，我觉得人们对佛教教义存在一种恐惧，担心如果不执着，就不会有足够的野心，也无法取得成功。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: If you're not anxiously chasing something.
turns.zh: 如果你不焦虑地追逐某些东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. If you're just like, "Why do I need that? I don't need to be the CEO of the VP because like, oh, I won't attach to that." And then, so people fear that downside. So I asked this question at this retreat and the advice they shared there was don't attach to this idea, but just point your cart in that direction and head there.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。如果你只是想：“我为什么需要那个？我不需要成为CEO或VP，因为……哦，我不会执着于此。” 然后，人们害怕这种负面影响。所以我在静修时问了这个问题，得到的建议是不要执着于这个想法，而是朝着那个方向前进。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Yeah, I like that. Look, the fear you're talking about is the fear of complacency. And if we look at the structures of the mind and we look at our socialization, the way we're socialized to ward off complacency is anxiety. And so, if we go back to some of the things we were saying before, if I grow up believing that the way I'm going to make my parents love me is by achieving, then if I become complacent, then what's at risk is their love for me. So just like we made the connection before where unconditional love exists, unconditional positive regard for self, otherwise known as self-compassion can be a powerful motivator, especially when you get to the point where you say, "As painful as it is for me to write, I enjoy writing. I enjoy working out. I enjoy pushing myself. I don't necessarily enjoy it in the moment." But I certainly, when I look at two books on my desk and I say, "You know what? That feels good. That makes me happy." (01:10:43): To me, the ability to hold the seeming contradiction of those things is a hallmark of my adulthood. It's to get satisfaction out of hard work for me is a much greater motivator than fear of complacency. As I've sort of slip-slided my way into that place, I have found... I work seven days a week. I don't have to, but I enjoy it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我喜欢这种说法。听着，你所说的恐惧是害怕自满。如果我们审视大脑的结构和社会化进程，就会发现社会化过程中用来抵御自满的手段就是焦虑。所以，回到我们之前讨论的部分——如果我从小就认为要获得父母的爱，就必须靠出色表现，那么当我变得自满时，父母对我的爱就会面临风险。正如我们之前提到的，无条件的爱、对自我的积极接纳（即自我同情）能成为强大的动力源泉，尤其是当你意识到“写作虽然痛苦，但我享受写作的过程；锻炼虽然艰难，但我乐在其中；我并不享受当下的过程”时。但当我看到桌上的两本书，心想“这感觉真好，这让我很开心”，对我而言，能承受这些看似矛盾的情绪正是成年人特有的标志。对我来说，从努力工作中获得满足感远比恐惧自满更有意义。当我逐渐习惯这种生活节奏时，发现……我每周工作七天。其实没必要这样，但我乐在其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's another, maybe a last area I want to spend some time on, which is around teams and what often causes trouble for teams. What breaks teams? What breaks companies? You have this point, you make that it's rarely lack of talent on the team, lack of strategy, lack of execution, that it's something else. What is that something else? What often do you find as the source of the problem for teams that aren't working?
turns.zh: 接下来我想再花点时间讨论团队问题，以及团队常遇到的难题。是什么让团队分崩离析？是什么让公司走向衰落？你提到团队的问题通常不是因为缺乏人才、缺乏战略或执行力不佳，而是其他原因。那么这个“其他原因”具体是什么？对于那些运转不畅的团队，你通常会发现哪些深层问题？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Well, it's the unresolved, I'll be dramatic with the language, demons from their childhood. It's the unsorted baggage. Here's what happens. Teams are groups, and there are group dynamics that always happen. There is the scapegoat, there is the truth-teller who has to say, "Let me tell you what's really wrong with everything going on." Without the individual's radical self-inquiry skills, groups tend to be condemned to repeating patterns oftentimes of their family of origin. (01:12:40): I'll tell you a quick story. There's a very famous software blogger, blogger-owned software that I coached for many years, and we were doing an executive team meeting, and something happened in the group as we were talking that I observed once, twice, and three times, and finally, I said, "Okay, guys, I'm seeing something happen here. Every time we get close to talking about something that's really painful, somebody makes a joke and all the energy disappears and everybody laughs and everybody's nice." And as soon as I said it, my client who was CEO at the time said, "Jesus Christ, that's just like my family." It was like, yes, that's just like your family. (01:13:35): Carl Jung once said, "Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate." Let's apply it here. Until you make conscious the unconscious patterns operating in the group, the group will continue to repeat those patterns and you will blame somebody in the group. Romantic relationships from a Buddhist perspective, part of what we do in romantic relationships is we find the perfect foil for us to work out our unconscious phenomena. When we join a group, when we form up in teams and organizations, we are unconsciously finding the perfect foils for us to work out our own shit. So if you want to create a high-functioning team, do your work, and it starts with the person who has the most power in the group. If that person refuses to do their work, the entire group will become a manifestation of early dysfunction in the individual's lives. Does that make any sense?
turns.zh:
嗯，这就是未解决的创伤，用夸张点的说法，就是童年时期的恶魔。这些未处理的包袱会引发一系列问题。团队是群体，群体动态总是会出现一些问题。比如，有个替罪羊，还有个直言不讳的人，总要说出“告诉你真正的问题所在”。如果团队成员缺乏深刻的自我反思能力，他们往往会陷入重复的模式，往往是源自童年家庭的模式。（01:12:40）：我讲个小故事。有个我指导多年的知名软件博主，他曾带领一个高管团队开会。每次谈论到敏感话题时，总有人开玩笑，气氛瞬间轻松，大家笑成一团。这时，我当时的客户（CEO）会感慨：“天啊，这简直就是我家的情况。”是啊，这就是你家庭的缩影。

（01:13:35）：卡尔·荣格曾说：“除非你将无意识变为有意识，否则它将掌控你的生活，而你却称之为命运。” 让我们把这句话应用到团队中。除非你将团队中无意识的模式显性化，否则团队会不断重复这些模式，而你只会归咎于某个成员。从佛教视角看恋爱关系，我们在亲密关系中寻找的完美伴侣，实质上是帮我们疗愈无意识创伤的载体。当我们加入团队、组建组织时，无意识地寻找能帮我们疗愈自身问题的伙伴。所以，若想打造高效团队，先从团队中最具权力的人开始。如果此人拒绝自我成长，整个团队将成为其童年创伤的延续。明白了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 100%. And this comes up a number of times on this podcast, just the impact the leaders issues have on the rest of the team, and also just this idea that the conditions they're trying to avoid are the conditions they invite in because they're avoiding.
turns.zh: 完全同意。这个播客中多次提到领导者的问题对团队的影响，还有一个观点：团队试图避免的状况，往往是他们刻意引入的。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: That's it. That's it. One of my favorite teachers and dear friends is Parker Palmer, and he builds on, I think it was Socrates who said, "The unexamined life is not worth living." And he builds on that and makes a joke, and he says, "But if you choose to live an unexamined life, please don't take a job that involves other people." And that's it. You have a responsibility to examine your own shit.
turns.zh: 就是这样。我最喜欢的老师兼挚友帕克·帕尔默曾引用苏格拉底的话：“未经审视的人生不值得过。”他以此为基础开玩笑道：“但如果你选择过未经审视的人生，请别从事需要与人打交道的工作。”这就是责任——审视自己的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So say you're on this team, so there's two sides of this. You're on a team, the leaders clearly got some stuff that they need to work through, but they're not. Is there something you can do there other than just, "Hey, please, this is hurting us?" And then from the leader's perspective listening to this, what should they do? Is it get a coach? What can you do?
turns.zh: 假设你身处这样的团队。问题有两方面：团队中有人明显有未解决的心理问题，但他们不愿面对。作为团队成员，除了说“拜托，这对我们有害”之外，你还能做什么？从领导者的角度听完这些，该怎么做？是请教练？还是别的什么？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: So for the one who has less power?
turns.zh: 那对于权力较弱的人呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: One of the things to ask oneself is what draws me to this position in the first place? How have I been complicit, not responsible in creating the conditions I say I don't want. How have I benefited from the dysfunction that exists in this organization? And benefit is a funny word. It doesn't necessarily mean I'm making more money. It means, for example, a benefit might be, boy, this feels familiar. I always find myself working on teams that are dysfunctional in this way. What is there in that experience for me to learn? So that's one thing. (01:16:55): You asked about the person who has power. You were using the word leader. I will talk about power, and you threw out, well, should they get a coach? Let's put it into larger context. Should you examine your life with radical self-inquiry? Yes. I would argue that the more power you have, the more moral responsibility you have to actually pause and figure out what it is that you're doing to be complicit in creating the conditions you say you don't want. (01:17:28): To be a very quick example what I'm talking about. A couple of years ago, I was doing a talk at a venture firm's CEO portfolio summit, the portfolio company's CEO summit. And we're sitting in a room, and of course I'm walking around again with shoes off and whatever, and people are firing questions at me. And one woman says, "Well, I'm the CEO of this 15-person company, and I have a question for you. Why is it that nobody on my team can make a decision without me?" And I said, "Who hired them?" And she, "Well..." I said, "Okay, how does it make you feel when they make a decision that you disagree with?" She said, "I'm furious." "Well, how can you hire people whom you expect to make decisions without running them through you if you can't tolerate them making a decision that you disagree with?" (01:18:37): You want to build a scaled leadership team, you have to be willing to have them make boneheaded decisions. And that's really, really hard, especially if we're "in founder mode" driving all the decisions. So that's your growth edge. We were talking about before about growth mindset. That's your growth edge. How can I be with the people in my life making boneheaded decisions about something that I care so much about and what is the best way for me to be in relationship about that?
turns.zh:
需要自问的一个问题是，究竟是什么吸引我选择了这份工作？我为何会默许甚至纵容自己创造出那些自己明明不想要的职场环境？我又从这种职场失序中获益了什么？这里的“获益”是个微妙的词，它不一定意味着赚得更多，而是指某种共鸣。比如当我发现自己总在混乱的团队中工作，总被动地应付问题时，这种共鸣感就油然而生。这种经历对我又有何启发？这就是第一个问题。

（01:16:55）：你问到拥有权力的人。我用了“领导者”这个词来指代权力持有者。我想谈谈权力问题。你提到是否该给他们请教练？让我们从更宏观的角度看待这个问题。你是否该用彻底的自我审视来审视自己的生活？是的。我认为权力越大，你就越有道德责任去停下来审视自己在助长职场乱象中扮演的角色。

（01:17:28）：举个快速例子说明我的观点。几年前，我在一家风投公司的CEO峰会上发言，参与者都是投资组合公司的CEO。我们围坐一室，我又光脚到处走，人们纷纷提问。一位女士问：“我是一家15人公司的CEO，我有个疑问——为什么团队成员做决策时非得经过我？”我反问：“谁雇佣了他们？”她说：“嗯……”我继续问：“当他们做出的决定与你的意见相左时，你作何感想？”她回答：“我很生气。”我追问：“如果连你都无法容忍他们做出的决定，又怎么能指望他们在未经你审核的情况下独立决策呢？”

（01:18:37）：如果你想组建一个有规模的领导团队，就必须允许他们做出错误决策。这真的很难，尤其当我们还处于“创始人模式”，亲自把控所有决策时。这就是你的成长契机。我们之前谈到的成长心态，这就是你的成长契机。如何与生活中那些在你极为关切的领域做出错误决策的人建立良性关系，又该如何以最佳方式处理这种关系？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So much of this comes back to that question we started this with of just how are you complicit in creating the conditions you don't want? A big takeaway for me here, and it just keeps coming up and again and again, is if you're struggling as a leader, if your company's not working as well as you wanted to, if you're having a hard time with your team, going back to that equation, it's not about building more skills like public speaking skills or email skills, or I don't know, financial skills. It's self-awareness, radical self-inquiry, understanding what drives you, what makes you happy. Is that generally correct?
turns.zh: 很多问题都回归到我们开场时提出的那个核心问题：你如何在无意中助长了自己不想要的职场环境？对我来说，一个重要启示——这个观点反复浮现——是如果作为领导者你深陷困境，如果公司发展不如预期，如果团队协作困难重重，归根结底不是要提升某项技能，比如公众演讲、邮件处理或财务管理技能。而是自我觉察、彻底的自我审视，理解自己的驱动力和快乐所在。这说得对吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Lenny, I was just going to say, you just made me so happy you saying what you just said. Yes. I've been coaching now, as I said for a couple of decades. Before that, I was a VC for 15, 17 years. What you just said is the wisdom of my 40 years as an adult. That's it. This is why radical self-inquiry is so damned important because it leads to a little bit less suffering and a lot more resilience.
turns.zh: 莱尼，我刚想说，你刚才说的话让我太开心了。是的。正如我所说，我做了几十年的教练。在此之前，我做了15、17年的风投。刚才你说的话，是我40年成人生活的智慧精华。这就是为什么彻底的自我审视如此重要，因为它能减少痛苦，增强韧性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that want to actually do that, well, they can rewind back to the middle of the episode where we actually ask the questions that are associated with the radical self-inquiry, and then obviously if they want to dig deeper, they can buy your book.
turns.zh: 想真正做到这一点的人，可以倒回去听剧集中间的部分，那时我们提出了与深度自我探索相关的问题。当然，如果他们想深入探讨，还可以购买你的书。

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Or 10 copies of the book.
turns.zh: 或者买10本这本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or 100 copies for everyone at the company willing to Amazon. Jerry, is there anything else that we haven't touched on that you think is really important for people to hear maybe as the last piece of wisdom?
turns.zh: 或者为公司里愿意在亚马逊上购买的每位员工买100本。杰瑞，你觉得还有什么我们没提到但对人们来说很重要、值得一听的智慧之言吗？

turns.speaker: Jerry Colonna
turns.en: Now one of the hopes that I have you ask me at the start like what would be my hope is that we ended up being closer and friends, and I feel that. Let me extend that out to everybody. What I always hope from all of these intimate conversations that I try to do in podcasts is that people walk away going, "Geez, I'm not alone." We've made different references to the fact that it's a hard time. The truth is it's always a hard time. And what makes it hardest is to feel like I'm the only one who's going through this. So what I appreciate about what you do, Lenny, is that under the guise of talking about product, you're really talking about the process of being human. And that is a mitzvah. That's a good deed. And so, I hope in the process of listening to this, people walk away going, "Okay, I feel a little bit better today."
